title: iCal in Mac OS X Lion, 2011
lede: Apple’s desktop calendar in Lion, with a stitched tan leather top bar and torn paper edges, the most cited example of the style’s excess.
summary: Stitched leather and torn desk-calendar pages on the Mac. Apple, 2011.

source.label: Apple, “Mac OS X Lion: New features” (archived July 2011)

made: 2011 (Mac OS X Lion); renamed Calendar in OS X Mountain Lion (2012); leather removed in OS X Mavericks (2013)

evidence.note: Apple’s archived Lion features page describes the “streamlined new look” of iCal; its screenshot of the app is only 323 × 199 px, too small to describe. The leather design is documented by Fast Company (2012) and by the style record’s sources.

styles.note: The emblematic example of the style: a desk calendar with leather binding, stitching, and torn pages, all without function.

context: Apple’s Lion page said iCal “features a streamlined new look that gives you more room to browse and edit your events.” [Apple, archived July 2011](https://web.archive.org/web/20110727225723/http://www.apple.com/macosx/whats-new/features.html).

A former senior Apple UI designer told Fast Company that “iCal’s leather-stitching was literally based on a texture in his Gulfstream jet,” meaning Steve Jobs’s jet. [Fast Company, Austin Carr, “Will Apple’s Tacky Software-Design Philosophy Cause A Revolt?” (2012)](https://www.fastcompany.com/1670760/will-apples-tacky-software-design-philosophy-cause-a-revolt).

Wikipedia’s lead on skeuomorphs uses “a software calendar that imitates the appearance of binding on a paper desk calendar” as its virtual example, citing Wired (2012). [Wikipedia: Skeuomorph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skeuomorph).
interpretation: The leather is decoration from a luxury interior, not from a calendar. That is why critics used it as the clearest sign of the style going too far.
